entry.title: Looping Inside the Experts, and Where the Gains in Recurrent Mixture-of-Experts Models Come From

link.title: Looping Inside the Experts, and Where the Gains in Recurrent Mixture-of-Experts Models Come From

entry.content:
During my work in the Pehlevan Lab this October, I tested an idea that felt like it should work: what if each expert in a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model could loop?

Looped transformers reuse the same layers several times, buying extra computation without extra parameters, and recent work like SMELT shows this can pay off even when FLOPs are matched. MoE models send each token to a few experts out of many. Putting the two together, I let each routed expert run several passes on its token: a short attention read followed by an FFN, repeated n times, with the result written back to the residual stream. Two things made this attractive. First, the router could in principle choose how many loops each token gets from each expert, so harder tokens would think longer. Second, under expert parallelism a token already travels to its expert’s GPU once per layer, so every extra loop runs there with no extra communication.

I couldn’t find this design in the (rather crowded) looped-MoE literature, so I spent a few weeks and around 480 training runs on it. It doesn’t pay off. How it fails turned out to be more interesting than the architecture itself, so this post is about that.

The Setup

All language-modeling runs use the same small model: 6 layers, width 384, 16 experts per layer with top-2 routing, the Mistral tokenizer, and 1B tokens of SlimPajama. Every model has 77.4M to 77.9M stored parameters; when a design adds parameters (say, attention inside the experts), I narrow its expert FFNs to keep the total equal. I report validation cross-entropy, count FLOPs per token analytically relative to the standard MoE, and use 3 seeds wherever a comparison hinges on it, since the seed-to-seed standard deviation is 0.001 to 0.008.

The baselines matter a lot here. Normalizing each expert’s output with an RMSNorm and a zero-initialized gain (which turns out to be exactly Peri-LN’s output norm) is worth 0.023 for free, so the fair baseline is a standard MoE with it, at 3.3775. The looping baselines are SMELT-style looping, where the middle three of six layers run twice (3.3464 at 1.26x FLOPs; unlike the paper, I don’t resize the model to match FLOPs), and block looping, where the whole stack runs twice (3.3505 at 1.53x).

Key Results

  • The original design, where each expert attends only to the tokens routed to the same expert, doesn’t beat the standard MoE at any loop count, and routers never learned to give harder tokens more loops.
  • Letting expert attention read the whole sequence helps (3.3354 vs 3.3775), but adding the same attention unrouted does just as well (3.3363). The gain comes from one extra attention step, and routing it into experts adds nothing.
  • Looping the same expert is the worst way to spend extra expert compute. Running 4 experts once (3.2961) beats routing to 2 new experts for a second round (3.3048), which beats looping the same 2 experts with or without refreshed context (3.3109 and 3.3206).
  • On a synthetic multi-hop task, a second pass that reads refreshed context chains about twice as many hops as layer looping at similar compute (38 vs 17 to 19).
  • On multi-step tasks written as text, that advantage disappears: SMELT-style and block looping are the most reliable designs there.

Attention Was Doing the Work

The first version gave each expert attention over only the tokens routed to the same expert, about an eighth of the context, so that loops never leave the expert’s GPU. It doesn’t beat the baseline at any loop count: n = 1, 2 and 4 land at 3.3832, 3.3732 to 3.3777, and 3.3809, against 3.3775. Letting the router choose loop counts didn’t rescue it either. Whether it scored (expert, loop count) pairs or used Mixture-of-Recursions-style capacity routing, the loop counts it chose never tracked how hard a token was: on a synthetic task where I know each token’s difficulty, the correlation stayed between -0.21 and +0.26. Halting gates fitted afterwards on models trained with random depth did learn difficulty on that synthetic task, but gave nothing on language modeling.

The bottleneck was the narrow attention. Giving each expert a query that reads the whole sequence, with keys and values computed once per layer and shared by all experts, brings a single pass down to 3.3354. That’s a big gain, but it’s the kind that needs controls, since the design now does more attention than the baseline. So I added the same attention unrouted, as a small extra attention sublayer in front of a standard MoE, along with the other obvious ways to spend the same budget.

The unrouted version matches it to within noise. It also beats spending the same budget on depth, with 7- and 8-layer standard MoEs at equal parameters and FLOPs, and beats a routed attention sublayer in the style of MoA. The architecture itself is close to prior work like MoA and UMoE, so the controlled comparison is the new part. The same thing shows up from the other direction: SMELT-style looping without re-running attention in its second pass loses its whole gain (3.3796, against 3.3496 with attention and 3.3775 for the standard MoE). The extra attention step over updated states is what helps.

At 4x the width and tokens, full-context experts with 4 loops still beat the normalized standard MoE by the same margin as at the base scale (0.055 at both), although I didn’t run the unrouted control at that scale.

Looping the Same Expert Is the Worst Use of Compute

With full-context attention in place, the real question for this project is what to do with a second unit of expert compute, at equal parameters and about 1.44x FLOPs. You can loop the same two experts again; loop them after rebuilding the shared keys and values from every token’s updated state (I’ll call this refreshed context); route the token to two new experts for a second round, as in Chain-of-Experts; or just use four experts at once.

Width wins, new experts come second, and looping the same expert comes last. Taking the comparison apart (same or new experts, private or shared state, stale or refreshed context, 3 seeds each), new experts beat reused ones by 0.020 to 0.025, and refreshing the context only recovers 0.007 to 0.010 of that. A plain 10-layer standard MoE at the same compute lands right next to the best same-expert variant (3.3168 vs 3.3109, though only 1 seed).

The reason the second loop does so little shows up in its geometry. With stale context, each later loop’s update points almost the same way as the expert’s total update, with a cosine of 0.87 to 0.95 in trained models. The loop mostly makes the same update longer, and the expert’s output normalization then throws that length away.

More loops don’t fix it either: four loops land at 3.3222 (2.15x), no better than two.

Where a Refreshed Pass Does Win: Chained Lookups

Language modeling at this scale might simply not need many sequential steps, so I also trained on k-hop induction heads (Sanford, Hsu and Telgarsky, 2024). Each position has to report where a k-step pointer walk over earlier symbols lands, which takes k sequential lookups. I used 2-layer models on sequences of four independent 192-symbol segments, with k drawn uniformly from 0 to 64, and report the largest k a model solves, meaning token accuracy of at least 0.95 for every k up to it.

Here the ranking flips. A second pass that reads refreshed context, whether through the same experts or new ones, chains about twice as many hops as SMELT-style or block looping at similar compute: 38 hops at 1.87x with a 64-position attention window, against 19 and 17 at 1.99x. Width does worst among the 2.6x designs, and the same experts with stale context sit in between. At around 4x compute, though, block looping solves the whole task and is the cheapest way to do so. This was the one result where looping individual experts clearly beat strong baselines, so it was the one worth stress-testing.

…and Where It Stops Winning: Multi-Step Text

To check whether the k-hop advantage means anything closer to real use, I built four multi-step tasks written as plain text, each with a difficulty d equal to the number of facts the answer has to chain through:

  • Variable tracking, in the style of RULER: 128 statements like “VAR x = 4721.” and “VAR y = x.”, then “What is the value of y?”
  • Program tracing: 96 lines like “let y = x * 2;”, then the value of a variable.
  • Multi-hop facts: “Ann’s boss is Beth. Beth lives in Rome.” and so on for 36 people, then “Where does Ann’s boss live?” (d = 2).
  • Graph reachability: 128 edges like “a -> b.”, then “Is there a path from s to t?”

Each language-model checkpoint was fine-tuned on all four at once for 10k steps, with 4 questions per example and the answers scored by exact match.

Every design handles single lookups. Chaining two is where they split: the standard MoE does it on two-hop facts in only 1 of 3 seeds, while SMELT-style and block looping do it in all three and also get the furthest at d = 3. Refreshed loops sit in between and depend a lot on the seed. One seed solves variable tracking through d = 4, which nothing else does, while another stays at 0.56 on two-hop facts. The windowed refreshed variant, the cheapest k-hop winner, is the least reliable of the five. Nothing reliably goes past three hops, and the roughly 2x edge from k-hop doesn’t carry over to these tasks, at least at this scale.

A Side Lesson: Making These Tasks Learnable

Getting a 78M-parameter model to learn these tasks at all took two tries, which is maybe the most practically useful part of this post. In the first version, every example asked one question with d drawn uniformly, and in 20k steps almost no design learned even d = 1 (the one exception was a single task for a single design). The models guessed a plausible value from the context instead, which showed up in a funny way: variable-tracking accuracy went up with d, since longer target chains leave fewer distinct values in the context to guess from. Sampling easy questions more often fixed single lookups but not two-hop ones (0.14 on two-hop facts).

What worked was asking every kind of single lookup on its own (“Who is Ann’s boss?”, “What is y set to?”), so each step a longer question composes gets direct training signal, and asking 4 questions per example. Training from scratch never left the guessing stage, even then. Synthetic tasks like k-hop sidestep all of this, since every position is a training target at every k, and I think that’s part of why results on them can look better than they turn out to be.

Why This Matters

Looped models are having a moment, and a lot of the proposals in this space, mine included, start from the intuition that reusing weights is what buys extra reasoning. At least at this scale, the thing doing the work was something else: another attention step over states that had already changed. That’s what full-context experts add over the baseline, what SMELT-style looping loses when it skips attention in the second pass, and what makes a refreshed second pass chain lookups. Whether that step happens inside a routed expert didn’t matter in any of my comparisons.

If you’re trying something similar, here’s what I’d take from this:

  • If you put attention inside MoE experts, compare against the same attention unrouted. In my runs it explains the whole gain.
  • If you have spare expert compute, spend it on more experts per token before spending it on loops of the same expert.
  • Refreshed context, not weight reuse, is what makes a second pass useful for multi-hop retrieval, and a local window keeps that cheap. But check on realistic tasks before trusting a synthetic multi-hop gain.
  • Routers that pick loop counts never learned to track token difficulty, and halting gates only helped on synthetic tasks.

Caveats

  • Everything is at one base scale (78M parameters, 1B tokens) with a single 4x check, and 1 to 3 seeds per result. The k-hop numbers are single seeds.
  • FLOPs are counted analytically, not measured in wall-clock time, and full-context expert attention also doubles the KV cache, which these numbers ignore.
  • The text tasks use small fine-tuned models, and larger pretrained models could well behave differently.
  • I haven’t tested turning an existing pretrained MoE into a looping one, so these results don’t say whether looping can be added to a model that was trained without it.

entry.summary: Letting each routed expert in an MoE loop on its token does not pay off. Where the gains come from instead: one extra attention step, more experts, and fresh context.

font-weight="600">2.37</text> <text x="302" y="207" class="t-muted" font-size="8.5" text-anchor="start">degree-tail exponent</text> </svg> </figure>
<p>During my work in the Pehlevan Lab over the Spring 2026 semester, I studied whether Mathlib, Lean’s library of formalized mathematics, has a measurable geometry, and whether that geometry tells AI theorem provers anything useful.</p>
<p>Mathematicians already talk about their field geometrically: some subjects are close together, some lemmas are central, some definitions are bottlenecks every later argument has to pass through. In a formal library, part of that language becomes data. Theorems cite other theorems, and tactics turn goals into subgoals. Barkeshli, Douglas, and Freedman recently proposed describing mathematics with proof hypergraphs, and I wanted to see what a real one looks like.</p>
<h3 id="the-setup">The Setup</h3>
<p>I built two graphs based on different notions of geometry from LeanDojo’s traces of Mathlib. The first is a theorem-dependency graph: an edge B → A means some tactic in B’s proof uses A as a premise. For Mathlib specifically, that comes around to a massive 138,333 nodes and 309,396 unique edges. The second is a state-tactic hypergraph, where nodes are proof states and each edge is a tactic taking one goal to its subgoals.</p>
<p>I then asked three questions: what the large-scale structure looks like, whether graph features predict properties of individual theorems, and whether paths through proof states can capture the idea that one theorem reduces to another.</p>
<h3 id="key-results">Key Results</h3>
<ul> <li>The dependency graph is highly structured. Its degree distribution is heavy-tailed (power-law tail exponent 2.37), Louvain finds 240 communities with modularity 0.592, and 50,191 of 61,544 traced proofs are linear. Locally, the graph looks tree-like and hub-driven.</li> <li>Local structure predicts proof length. Degree alone gets R² = 0.483 on log tactic count, and adding a node2vec embedding raises that to 0.555.</li> <li>Spectral coordinates are weak. They get R² = 0.003 on proof length, and predicting a theorem’s Mathlib area with spectral plus degree features gets 0.177 accuracy against a 0.165 majority baseline. The theorem’s namespace alone gets 0.737.</li> <li>As such, funnily enough, there’s an “autoformalization” problem here, where the same concepts can be expressed in many different ways in Lean, and it’s nontrivial to merge the true positives together.</li> </ul>
<p>The degree result is less impressive than it looks, since a longer proof has more chances to cite distinct premises. The node2vec gain on top of degree is the more interesting number. The pathfinding failure has a clear cause: <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">rw</code>, <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">simp</code>, and instantiation use a theorem without its statement ever becoming the current goal, so matching printed goals misses most real dependencies.</p>
<h3 id="why-this-matters">Why This Matters</h3>
<p>Before an AI system searches for proofs or proposes new lemmas inside Mathlib, it helps to know which parts of the library are central and which features track proof complexity. Graph geometry works as that kind of measurement. Theorem discovery from the graph will need a finer object, though: one that exposes what tactics like <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">rw</code> and <code class="language-plaintext highlighter-rouge">simp</code> do internally (matched subterms, instantiated lemmas, side goals), so that repeated proof transformations become visible and can be compressed into new lemmas.</p>
<p>As models get better at theorem discovery and autoformalization, in light of the many advances in this area in the last few months, being able to determine where in our understanding new proofs live, as well as more principled automatic discovery methods (such as, for example, exploring the sparsely populated regions of this graph) to point the LLMs towards become more and more valuable, and I hope this brings us one step closer to rigorous automatic science.</p>

entry.title: In-Context Learning Without Attention: MLP Mixers as an Alternative to Transformers

link.title: In-Context Learning Without Attention: MLP Mixers as an Alternative to Transformers

entry.content:
During my work in the Pehlevan Lab over the Spring 2025 semester, I investigated whether you really need attention mechanisms for in-context learning (ICL)—the ability of models to learn from examples in their input without updating parameters.

The prevailing wisdom says yes: attention seems essential for comparing information across positions. But recent work from Tong and Pehlevan showed even vanilla MLPs could learn in-context under certain conditions. This made me wonder about MLP Mixers, which achieve global information transfer through token-mixing operations rather than attention.

The Experiment

I used synthetic classification tasks based on Gaussian mixture models. Models had to infer cluster-to-label mappings from context examples and apply them to a query point. By varying the number of clusters (k) from 32 to 2048, I forced a transition from memorization to true in-context learning—with enough clusters, memorization becomes impossible.

Key Results

  • MLP Mixers matched Transformer performance while using 3x fewer parameters. My best Mixer had only 3,389 parameters compared to the Transformer’s 9,508.
  • The Mixer showed a sharp transition from memorization to ICL around 2^9 clusters.

However, the Transformer results were unexpected and somewhat concerning—it showed minimal improvement in ICL performance even at high cluster counts. This likely indicates the Transformer needed more parameters or different training dynamics, but it deserves deeper investigation before drawing strong conclusions.

What’s Next

I’m currently working on several follow-up directions:

  • Retraining with decoder-only Transformers to see if the architecture makes a difference
  • Comparing Mixer behavior to what Transformers actually do and what Gautam Reddy’s work predicts they should do
  • Borrowing methods from Reddy’s papers for more rigorous mechanistic analysis
  • Testing whether one layer and one head is sufficient for these tasks

The mechanistic interpretability remains elusive. Activation analysis suggests the Mixer focuses on context rather than query tokens, and attribution flows through limited channels, but the full picture of how information routes through the model needs more work.

Why This Matters

If Mixers can achieve comparable ICL with fewer parameters, that opens new architectural possibilities—especially important as training costs and energy consumption bottleneck large language models. The results suggest in-context learning might be more general than we thought, not intrinsically tied to attention mechanisms.

But the Transformer underperformance is a puzzle that needs solving before making strong claims.

Citation
